# Why Small Engine Ignition Coils Read as Open Circuits

When troubleshooting a gas-powered hedge trimmer or similar small engine, measuring an ignition coil that reads several kilohms (kÎ©) can be baffling if you expect a low-ohm reading like 50 Î©. The immediate reaction might be to assume the component is dead, but in the world of automotive and small engine electronics, "dead" often just means "working differently than a resistor."

To diagnose this correctly, you must distinguish between the primary winding and the secondary winding. These two circuits serve fundamentally different purposes and therefore exhibit vastly different resistance values. If your multimeter shows high resistance across the terminals that connect to the spark plug wire (or boot), you are measuring the secondary coil. This is not a fault; it is exactly how a functional ignition coil should behave.

## The Primary vs. Secondary Divide

Ignition coils operate on the principle of electromagnetic induction, utilizing two distinct windings wrapped around a laminated iron core. The **primary winding** consists of many turns of relatively thick copper wire. Its job is to handle the high current coming from the battery or magneto, typically 12V for small engines. Because the wire is thicker and has fewer turns, its DC resistance is low. You should expect a reading typically between 0.5 Î© and 3 Î© for the primary side.

The **secondary winding**, however, uses extremely fine enameled copper wire wrapped thousands of times around the core. This construction is necessary to step up voltage from roughly 12V to anywhere between 15,000V and 40,000V required to jump the spark plug gap. The sheer length of this fine wire creates significant DC resistance. A healthy secondary coil will almost always read between 6 kÎ© and 15 kÎ©.

If you are measuring across the terminals where the high-tension lead connects (the side with the spark boot) and seeing a value in the kilohms, your coil is likely intact. Conversely, if you measure near zero ohms across the secondary terminals, that indicates a shorted winding, which would prevent voltage buildup.

## Proper Diagnostic Procedure

The most common pitfall when testing these components is measuring the wrong pair of terminals or using an inappropriate multimeter setting. Here is the correct procedure to rule out a bad coil:

1.  **Isolate the Component**: Disconnect all spark plug boots and high-tension wires from the coil.
2.  **Identify Terminals**: Look for two distinct connection points. One set will be low resistance (primary), and the other will be high resistance (secondary). On many small engines, there is also a center terminal that might be grounded via the engine block, but modern coils often have isolated primary and secondary terminals on the same housing.
3.  **Measure Primary Resistance**: Set your multimeter to the 200 Î© range. Measure across the terminals labeled for battery connection (often marked + or B+). You should see a few ohms. If this reads infinity, the coil is open internally.
4.  **Measure Secondary Resistance**: Switch your multimeter to the 20 kÎ© or 200 kÎ© range. Measure across the terminals where the spark plug wire attaches. A reading between 6 kÎ© and 15 kÎ© confirms the secondary winding is functional.

### Multimeter Configuration Note
Ensure your multimeter is set to measure DC resistance (Ohms), not continuity with a buzzer, though both will work for this application. Avoid using Auto Range if possible; selecting a fixed range ensures you can see decimal points clearly and avoids jumping between scales which might cause confusion during the diagnosis.

## Troubleshooting the Real Issue

If your hedge trimmer fails to start but the coil resistance checks out perfectly on both windings, the issue lies elsewhere in the ignition system. The high tension wire itself often degrades internally, presenting infinite resistance regardless of the coil's health. Additionally, if the primary side measures infinity (open circuit), the coil is definitely failed and requires replacement.

It is also worth noting that some older points-based systems or transistors integrated into the coil housing can fail even if the windings are good. A simple way to verify this is to check for a spark while cranking with the plug held near the engine block (observe carefully). If there is no spark despite correct resistance readings, inspect the ignition module or points for fouling or failure.

Understanding the distinction between primary and secondary windings prevents unnecessary part replacements and saves time when diagnosing stubborn small engines. The kilohm reading you observed is not a sign of failure; it is the expected characteristic of a healthy high-voltage step-up transformer.
